content: The British Doctors Study is the widely recognized name for a prospective cohort study that was conducted from 1951 to 2001. In 1956, it provided robust statistical evidence that tobacco smoking significantly increased the risk of developing lung cancer. Although there had been suspicions of a connection between smoking and various diseases, the evidence supporting this link was largely circumstantial at the time. Smoking had even been marketed as healthy for many years, and there was no clear explanation for the dramatic rise in lung cancer rates. To investigate this potential link further, the Medical Research Council (MRC) tasked its Statistical Research Unit (later known as the Oxford-based Clinical Trial Service Unit) with conducting a prospective study. This approach to addressing medical questions was relatively novel at the time. In their 1954 Preliminary Report, the researchers felt it necessary to define the concept of the prospective principle. When the study was published in 1956, it marked the beginning of a new era in scientific research, highlighting the importance of epidemiology and medical statistics in addressing public health issues. Crucially, it established a definitive link between tobacco smoking and several serious diseases. In October 1951, the researchers contacted all registered male physicians in the United Kingdom, receiving responses from approximately two-thirds of them, totaling 34,439 participants. No additional cohorts were recruited after this initial group. The respondents were categorized by decade of birth, and their cause-specific mortality, general physical health, and current smoking habits were monitored through follow-up questionnaires in 1957, 1966, 1971, 1978, 1991, and finally in 2001. The response rates to these questionnaires were high, enabling robust statistical analyses. The results demonstrated that both lung cancer and coronary thrombosis (the term then used for myocardial infarction) occurred significantly more frequently in smokers. Subsequent follow-up reports, published every ten years, provided additional insights. One major conclusion of the study was that smoking reduces life expectancy by up to 10 years. Furthermore, more than 50% of all smokers die from diseases known to be related to smoking. The degree of excess mortality depends on the duration of smoking. For instance, individuals who quit smoking by age 30 experience no excess mortality, those who quit by age 40 lose an average of 1 year of life, those who quit by age 50 lose an average of 4 years, and those who quit by age 60 lose an average of 7 years. The true impact of the study is difficult to quantify, as smoking was not considered a public health issue in the 1950s, and awareness of the problem only grew in subsequent decades. Nevertheless, the British Doctors Study provided conclusive evidence linking smoking to lung cancer, myocardial infarction, respiratory diseases, and other smoking-related illnesses. The original study was led by Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill. Richard Peto joined the team in 1971 and, alongside Doll, prepared all subsequent reports for publication. Both Doll and Peto are celebrated epidemiologists, and their pioneering work on this study is a significant part of their legacy. They continued their research on other cardiovascular studies, such as the more recent Heart Protection Study.
